research.digest:
What this event is. A one-day, approval-only AGI House build day co-hosted by Google DeepMind as the finale of Open Source AI Week: about 100-120 curated builders in teams of 3-4, Oct 24, listed as 10:00-17:00 PT with doors at 9:30. The only hard rule is Gemma-based and fully on-device, "no cloud anywhere in the loop". Judging is science-fair style at the workbenches, then the top six teams demo on stage before awards. No rubric, judge list, demo length or submission checklist is public; submissions go through AGI House's own platform under two tracks (Mobile AI; Physical AI/Robotics/Embedded), and the projects tab sits behind Google sign-in. Pre-building is not just allowed, it is assumed: attendees are selected for what they have already built on hardware and told to bring their robot. With roughly six hours on site, nothing that is not working on Oct 23 will work on Oct 24.

Money. Four $15k pools (Best in Show Android+Pixel; Track 1 Mobile; Track 2 Physical AI, each 7.5/5/2.5k; Best Use of LiteRT 7.5/5/2.5k), plus hardware awards (2x Pixel 11, 5x Pi 5, 5x Coralboard, Qualcomm kits built around the Arduino VENTUNO Q/UNO Q). Both track winners get the "Break Glass" trophy. Whether one project can take Track 2 plus LiteRT plus a hardware award is unstated here; at Google's own Kaggle Gemma hackathons stacking a main prize with a technology prize is explicitly allowed and happened (Gemma Vision won 1st and the AI Edge prize). Realistic target for the G1: Track 2 first ($7.5k + trophy) plus Best Use of LiteRT ($7.5k) if LiteRT-LM is genuinely in the loop; Best in Show and the Pixel prize need an Android app on a Pixel and are a separate project.

How Google's Gemma people judge. The same small panel runs every Gemma hackathon (Glenn Cameron, Kristen Quan, Gus Martins, Ian Ballantyne, Omar Sanseviero, Kat Black) with a published rubric of Impact & Vision 40, Storytelling 30, Technical Depth 30, an explicit ask for a "wow factor", and a stated intent to verify the tech is real and "not just faked for the demo". Their winners posts praise closed-loop data engines, auditable reasoning, offline operation, privacy, and "disciplined, non-hallucinatory design". Their 2026 first prize out of 1,605 entries was a robot: GEM-4, a wearable arm VLA with a Gemma 4 E2B backbone, voice wake word, local Jetson inference and a human-video-to-robot-data pipeline. Their 2025 Jetson prize went to an Orin NX 16GB voice companion (Whisper + VAD + Gemma + Piper, <5 s, 15-25 W, wake-word trick to hide cold start). Google's own flagship robot demo is Reachy Mini on a Pi 5: fully local YOLO + Moonshine STT + Gemma 4 E2B via LiteRT-LM (99 prefill / 9 decode tok/s) + streaming TTS and gestures. Expect judges to benchmark you against that mentally; a humanoid that perceives, talks and manipulates locally clears it by a wide margin if it is reliable.

Likely judges and interests. Ian Ballantyne (Gemma DevX lead, built the Reachy demo) and Matthias Grundmann (Google AI Edge, LiteRT) are speaking in San Jose at Arm Create on Oct 19 (free, waitlist); going there is the cheapest way to meet them, show a phone video of the G1, and ask how the day is scored. Glenn Cameron and Kristen Quan write the winners posts, so a project that is easy to describe in two sentences helps. Hardware partners (NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Pi, Synaptics, Android) likely pick their own awards.

Gotchas. (1) Voice demos in a 100-person house: use a close-talk or beamforming mic and a push-to-talk fallback. (2) LiteRT-LM has no CUDA path; on Orin the GPU route is the WebGPU accelerator, which community reports say works on Orin NX 16GB (about 1.9 s per short prompt in April; segfaults mid-year; a Sept 14 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround) at far lower throughput than llama.cpp, so the LiteRT award costs latency; a hybrid (llama.cpp for the fast perception loop, LiteRT-LM for the voice/skills layer, or LiteRT-LM on a Pi 5 or VENTUNO Q side-board) is a legitimate way to qualify. (3) AGI House's robotics crowd (DeepMind's Stuart Bowers, NVIDIA's Marco Pavone, Zoox, Optimus staff) discounts controlled-setting clips and teleop; have a success-rate table and show a failure and recovery. (4) Google's rubric is 70 percent story and impact; the stage demo should be a 2-3 minute narrative with a protagonist, and a backup video must exist.

Ranked, what judges reward: 1) a working end-to-end loop on real hardware in front of them, all local; 2) visible use of Gemma 4-specific features (native audio, vision, function calling, E2B at low latency) rather than a wrapper; 3) an inspiring, human-centered story (accessibility and assistance recur in every winners list); 4) honest numbers and a failure/recovery moment; 5) LiteRT-LM or partner silicon in the loop for the side awards; 6) clean repo and a shareable video. What they penalize: anything cloud-touching (disqualifying), demos that only run from a laptop recording, overclaiming autonomy, a Gemma that could be swapped for any model, and projects with no clear user.

All six claims hold against the official pages, which I read directly in the browser (the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted this turn, so no additional searching was possible). Change these assumptions:

1. The Kaggle 40/30/30 rubric belongs to video-judged online contests. research.digest:
What exists. Pixel 11 (Tensor G6, 12 GB, $899/256 GB), Pixel 11 Pro ($1,099) and Pro XL ($1,299) have been on sale since Aug 20, 2026 and the Google Store is selling them now with a trade-in promo through Oct 29. Google's on-device LLM runtime for Android is LiteRT-LM (Kotlin artifact com.google.ai.edge.litertlm:litertlm-android, v0.18.0 released Oct 6, 2026); MediaPipe LLM Inference and the AI Edge Function Calling SDK are maintenance-only/deprecated in its favor. The decisive fact for us: Google publishes Pixel-TPU builds of Gemma 4 E2B for LiteRT-LM (gemma-4-E2B-it_Google_Tensor_G5.litertlm for Pixel 10, _Google_Tensor_G6 for Pixel 11; 4-bit, 8192 context), and an official Apache-2.0 sample, litert-samples/samples/litert/google/sample_app_tpu, that already does multimodal (text, image, audio-recording) chat on the Pixel 10 TPU with TPU→GPU→CPU fallback. Fork that: litertlm-android 0.12.0 (bump to 0.18.0), litert 2.3.0, minSdk 26, arm64 only, CameraX, JDK 21, jniLibs useLegacyPackaging=true. The Tensor ML SDK (beta May 2026; G6 support v2.0 Sep 2; v2.1 Oct 14) is only needed to compile your own models and requires a Linux x86_64 box; for Gemma 4 E2B you just download the prebuilt file.

Numbers. No Pixel-TPU tokens/s for Gemma 4 are public (the Tensor ML terms forbid publishing TPU performance data). Official LiteRT-LM reference points: S26 Ultra GPU 3808 prefill / 52 decode tok/s, TTFT 0.3 s at a 1024-token prefill; Qualcomm IQ8 NPU 3747/31.7/0.3 s; S26 Ultra CPU 557/47/1.8 s. MTP speculative decoding on GPU raised S26 decode to 66–92 tok/s. A Sep 30 Beebom test of the Gallery app (CPU only) got Pixel 11 Pro XL 271 prefill / 24.7 decode / 0.98 s TTFT vs Pixel 10 Pro 166 / 10.4 / 1.65 s. Expect Pixel 11 GPU to be S26-class and TPU to be prefill-heavy like IQ8; a ~300-token prompt plus a 70-token image plus a 15-token tool call should land well under a second on TPU/GPU, but measure on day one. Memory: 2.6–3.3 GB file plus ~0.7–1.7 GB peak; fine on 12 GB.

Modalities and tools. Gemma 4 E2B takes audio (multilingual ASR and speech translation, max 30 s clips, 16 kHz mono, 25 tokens per second) and images (70–1120 visual tokens), with native function calling and a thinking mode. LiteRT-LM Kotlin exposes Content.AudioBytes/AudioFile/ImageBytes/ImageFile, separate visionBackend/audioBackend, ToolSet with @Tool/@ToolParam, automaticToolCalling on/off, constrained decoding and ThinkingConfig. The AudioBytes PCM format is undocumented (community: 16 kHz mono 16-bit), so test it first. A Pixel 10a field report shows tool-call success dropping from ~90–100% at 0–1 args to 0% at 4 args, with GPU corrupting numbers in arguments while CPU did not; keep robot tools to ≤2 simple args, validate client-side and run a warm-up generation. This matches our llama.cpp findings on the Mac.

Gemini Nano alternative. ML Kit GenAI APIs on AICore (Prompt API beta: text+image; Speech Recognition alpha; Summarize/Rewrite/Image Description beta) run nano-v3 on Pixel 9/10 and nano-v4 on Pixel 11, and Google says Gemma 4 is what AICore ships as Gemini Nano. But the Prompt API has no audio input and no tool-calling API, and judges may not count "Gemini Nano" as a Gemma model, so use it only as a bonus. The one piece worth using is ML Kit Speech Recognition Advanced mode (Pixel 10/11 only): fully local streaming STT with high-accuracy en, ko, es, fr, de, it, pt, zh-Hans/Hant, ja, th, ru plus nine beta languages, which is better than feeding 30-second clips to Gemma. For TTS, Android's TextToSpeech with Google's engine has downloadable offline voices; LiteRT samples include Matcha-TTS and streaming KittenTTS; sherpa-onnx Piper/Kokoro is the community fallback.

Robot link. Keep everything on LAN: a small JSON-over-WebSocket server on the G1's PC2 bridging to unitree_sdk2 DDS, advertised with mDNS so the app finds it via NsdManager, with the Pixel sending high-level commands and receiving status/camera frames. Avoid Unitree's app WebRTC path (signaling via Unitree's cloud MQTT; G1 firmware ≥1.5.1 needs a per-device AES key); the Python unitree_webrtc_connect works in STA-L local mode if ever needed. Bring a travel router or use the phone hotspot so "no cloud" is verifiable.

Recommendation. Make the Pixel the robot's face, ears, mouth and planner: Gemma 4 E2B on the Pixel TPU (LiteRT-LM) takes mic audio and camera frames, answers in the user's language, and emits ≤2-arg tool calls (go_to, look_at, grasp, hand_over) that the app ships over LAN to the Orin, which runs our existing Gemma 4 perception loop. That one build is eligible for Best in Show (Android + Pixel end-to-end), Best Use of Pixel/TPU, Best Use of LiteRT and the Physical AI track. Buy a Pixel 11 ($899) rather than a Pixel 10 unless a 16 GB Pixel 10 Pro deal matters; both have prebuilt TPU files. Android XR glasses ship "later this fall" with no date, so they are not an option; Pixel Watch 5 can only be a wake trigger.
open_questions: Pixel TPU throughput for Gemma 4 E2B is unpublished: install sample_app_tpu with the _Google_Tensor_G6 file on day one, log which backend initialized, and measure TTFT and decode for a ~300-token prompt + one 480x336 image + a short tool call on NPU vs GPU vs CPU (note the Tensor ML terms bar publishing these numbers).

Whether the vision and audio encoders of the G6 TPU build run on the TPU or fall back to GPU/CPU (EngineConfig visionBackend/audioBackend): check the sample's LiteRTLMManager logs and time an image turn vs a text-only turn.
Exact PCM format for Kotlin Content.AudioBytes (community says 16 kHz mono 16-bit): read the Gallery's Audio Scribe recorder code and confirm transcription of a 5 s clip works.

Does the Play Store Gallery app use the Tensor TPU on Pixel 10/11? (Beebom's Sep 30 test ran CPU-only; search budget ran out before I could check.) Install Gallery and look at its accelerator picker; if it lacks TPU, that is also a judge-facing differentiator for our app.

Will judges accept Gemini Nano/AICore (ML Kit Prompt API) as 'a Gemma-based model'? Google's docs say AICore ships Gemma 4 as Gemini Nano, but the safe path is explicit Gemma 4 weights via LiteRT-LM; ask the organizers before building anything on the Prompt API.

Bay Area in-store availability of Pixel 11 was not verified (Best Buy pages are bot-blocked; the Google Store page showed pricing but no shipping ETA): check bestbuy.com store pickup for Pixel 11 256 GB or order from the Google Store today.

Whether a sideloaded APK that bundles libLiteRtDispatch_GoogleTensor.so (from the litert 2.3.0 / litert-npu-runtime-google-tensor Maven artifacts) is covered by the Tensor ML terms' distribution clause (§4.16) for a hackathon demo; the official sample is Apache-2.0, so demoing is presumably fine, but do not publish TPU benchmarks.
ML Kit Speech Recognition Advanced mode on Pixel 11 in airplane mode: confirm the model downloads once and then recognizes offline, and that the phone's bootloader is locked (unsupported otherwise).

G1 specifics: firmware version (≥1.5.1 changes WebRTC auth), whether PC2 can host our WebSocket server beside the DDS bridge, and whether the venue Wi-Fi allows phone-to-robot traffic (bring a travel router or use the Pixel hotspot).

Tool-call reliability for numeric arguments on the Pixel GPU/TPU backends (the Pixel 10a report saw corruption on GPU): run our bench prompts through the app with automaticToolCalling=false and count malformed calls per backend.

I could not read the Android SpeechRecognizer and Voice reference pages (the fetch returned only navigation), so framework on-device STT/TTS API details are from general knowledge; the ML Kit speech API and TextToSpeech offline voices are the documented paths.

verify.corrections: All six claims survive, but change these assumptions. (1) Audio format is settled, not a community rumor: Google's own apps feed Gemma 4 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM. The AI Edge Gallery passes raw PCM (no WAV header, SAMPLE_RATE = 16000, clips capped at 30 s) as Content.AudioBytes; the Pixel-TPU sample writes a 16 kHz/mono/16-bit WAV and passes Content.AudioFile. Both set audioBackend = CPU. (2) The TPU sample is Pixel 10-only on paper: it tries the NPU only when NPU is the chosen preference and com.google.android.aicore is installed, bundles libLiteRtDispatch_GoogleTensor.so in jniLibs, caps images at one per turn, and pins litertlm-android 0.12.0 (current 0.18.0, served from Google Maven, not Maven Central; expect API drift). Tensor G6 support arrived with Tensor SDK v2.0 (Sep 2, 2026) and a public runtime, com.google.ai.edge.litert:litert-npu-runtime-google-tensor:2.3.0, appeared Oct 6; the NPU guide lists E2B only on Tensor_G6 and says the Tensor SDK has no on-device compilation yet. Nobody citable has run E2B on a Pixel 11 TPU, so build the GPU/CPU fallback first and test the TPU on day one. (3) The Gallery runs Gemma 4 on gpu,cpu only, strips GPU on Pixel 10 (hence Beebom's CPU-only numbers), keeps it on Pixel 11, and stores models internally on Pixel 11 "CD1A" builds to avoid a FUSE DMA-mapping bug. (4) Tensor ML terms §4.17–4.18 forbid publishing Tensor performance data: keep TPU tok/s off slides. (5) Missed and useful: ConversationConfig.enableResponseFormat plus ResponseFormat (JSON Schema/regex via LLGuidance) gives constrained JSON for robot commands in Kotlin; EngineConfig.maxNumTokens sizes the KV cache; an undocumented Backend.GOOGLE_TENSOR exists on main. (6) Unverified: the Store trade-in promo (page never rendered) and the Function Calling SDK's deprecation (its docs and the ai-edge-apis repo now 404).

findings.claim: Gemma 4 E2B and E4B accept audio natively (ASR and speech-to-translated-text) via a 305M-parameter USM-style Conformer encoder processing 40 ms chunks of 16 kHz audio, with a 30-second maximum per clip; FLEURS WER is 0.080 (E2B) / 0.065 (E4B) for English and 0.090 / 0.075 averaged over en, ko, ja, de, fr, hi, es, it, pt-br, ru, ar, zh.
findings.evidence: The official model card lists audio on E2B/E4B/12B only, 'Audio supports a maximum length of 30 seconds', ASR and AST prompt templates. The Gemma 4 technical report gives the 305M encoder, 40 ms chunks, FLEURS and CoVoST (BLEU 35.4 / 38.2) numbers.

findings.claim: llama.cpp supports Gemma 4 audio input: PR #21421 (merged 2026-04-12) added the conformer encoder for llama-mtmd-cli (--mmproj ... --audio file.wav), PR #21824 fixed garbled E2B transcripts (causal attention), and llama-server accepts OpenAI-style `input_audio` {data: base64, format: wav} blocks on /v1/chat/completions (a build-9493 mmproj-loading regression was closed 2026-06-04 via PR #24091). Quality is uneven: a CUDA user measured RTF ~0.04 with E4B Q4_K_M and E2B BF16 but E2B Q8_0 leaked thinking tokens (RTF 0.31, HTTP 500s); an 8 GB M2 Ollama test got loops and hallucinations on Japanese.
findings.evidence: PR #21421 shows the CLI example and recommends a BF16 mmproj at 16 kHz; issue #21820 (E2B wrong transcripts) closed by #21824; issue #24084 closed with a commenter confirming input_audio transcription matched whisper.cpp on a 6 s clip. The dev.to .NET write-up reports the server request shape and RTF; the note.com test reports failures on Japanese via Ollama 0.20.2.

findings.claim: Gemma 4 object detection is documented as prompt 'detect X and Y' returning a JSON list of {"box_2d": [y1, x1, y2, x2] on a 0-1000 grid, "label"}; at the 70-token image budget Google's own example finds 2 of 6 objects versus 6 at 280 tokens, so cluttered table scenes need 140-280 tokens or a crop. research.digest:
What made humanoid+LLM demos land, and what made service robots boring. Figure 01 (2024), Helix (2025), Digit's LLM demo and Google's Apollo demos all share three things: language that is visibly grounded in what the robot sees at that moment, a completed physical act (apple handover, grocery pass between robots, box moved), and credible autonomy. Tesla's We Robot and 1X NEO lost the room the instant teleoperation was suspected. Pepper, temi and the Henn-na Hotel staff were retired because they talked but neither understood people nor touched objects. For six judges rotating science-fair style, the winning shape is therefore: a judge speaks (in any language), the robot shows it heard and saw correctly within about a second, then does one unmistakable physical thing, with no laptop operator in the loop. Google's own event copy ("learns a chore from watching you once") echoes the Oct 14 Gemini 4 Argon cornhole demo and Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 (<200 examples, hours of adaptation, early access only); neither is reproducible in six days, but a SeeDo-style version is.

What runs where. Speech in: Gemma 4 E2B/E4B hear 16 kHz audio up to 30 s through a 305M conformer; FLEURS WER is 8.0%/6.5% English and 9.0%/7.5% across 12 languages including zh, ja, ko, es, hi, ar. llama.cpp has it (PR #21421 merged April 12, E2B fix #21824, llama-server `input_audio` working by June) and one CUDA user measured RTF ~0.04 with E4B Q4_K_M, but E2B Q8_0 leaked thinking tokens (RTF 0.3, HTTP 500s), a Japanese test via Ollama looped and hallucinated, and Jetson AI Lab flags "an audio issue with E2B under llama.cpp" and points to its vLLM container for audio on Orin. So: headline the single-model story (Gemma hears, sees, decides) but ship a tested fallback. On the G1's own Orin NX, faster-whisper base fp16 does a 5.5 s utterance in 0.37 s; sherpa-onnx lists Orin NX with GPU and bundles Whisper, Parakeet v3 (25 European languages, not streaming), Moonshine, VAD, and text-defined keyword spotting with no training. Speech out: Piper (39 languages, no Japanese/Korean, fast on CPU, binary works on aarch64) is the safe default; Kokoro has better English and Japanese but its Mandarin voices are graded D and it is slow on small CPUs. The G1 speaker is reachable via AudioClient.PlayStream over DDS; Unitree's own TtsMaker exists too.

Audio capture is the known time sink. Marvik spent a month on it: the G1's 4-mic array picks up Jetson, motor-driver and vibration noise and software fixes did not help; an external USB mic placed away from the electronics did. Their custom openWakeWord model hit 57% recall with 11 false wakes per hour, so they switched to Porcupine. In a loud hall, use a ReSpeaker XVF3800 (USB Audio Class 2.0, AEC, beamforming, direction-of-arrival to the host, 5 m) mounted on the chest, or clip a USB-class-compliant wireless lavalier on the judge, and keep push-to-talk (a button on the robot, or the judge's phone over our own AP) as the zero-risk path. Direction-of-arrival from the array is a free "turn to face whoever spoke" primitive.

Vision: our box_2d path already scores 100% at 378 ms at 70 image tokens on the Mac, and Google's doc shows the 70-token budget misses objects in clutter (2 of 6 versus 6 at 280), so use 140-280 tokens or a crop for table scenes. NanoOWL's famous 95 FPS is AGX-only with no NX number and community reports of seconds per frame when misconfigured; Grounding DINO 1.5 Edge is API-gated; YOLO-World worldv2 with set_classes exports to TensorRT but has no Jetson figure (closed-set YOLO26n is 4 ms on NX). Recommendation: keep Gemma 4 as the only perception model for the demo logic and add YOLO-World only if a 10 Hz tracker proves necessary.

Robot primitives available today without learning: Move(vx, vy, vyaw), WaveHand, ShakeHand, and 16 canned arm actions (hug, high five, clap, heart, hands up, reject...). Reaching needs the xr_teleoperate pinocchio IK plus a D435i depth target; no sourced autonomous G1 tabletop grasp exists, and RealSense on Orin NX under JetPack 6 needs a source build. Treat grasp as the risk item and design the demo so everything before it already impresses.

Feasibility-ranked primitives (stack in parentheses): 1) voice Q&A about the live scene with gesture replies (ext. mic, PTT or sherpa KWS, Gemma 4 audio+image via llama-server or faster-whisper fallback, Piper, AudioClient, ExecuteAction) - high. 2) multilingual understanding and reply (Gemma 4 ASR/AST; Piper for es/zh/fr/de/hi/ar, Kokoro for ja) - high, verify each language on the shipped quant. 3) gestures - trivial, but verify WaveHand on our firmware. 4) point at / identify objects (box_2d to bearing, turn plus say) - high. 5) walk-to-person (box_2d bearing and box height, Move until LiDAR/depth stop distance, person with the remote on L2+B) - medium-high. 6) learn-from-watching (hand-speed keyframes, Gemma 4 lists objects and steps, map to existing primitives, replay with pointing or a simple pick-place) - medium; keep to 2-3 steps. 7) grasp a known object from a table (depth, IK, fixed-height close on a soft can) - medium-low. 8) handover (extend arm, release when a hand is detected) - depends on 7.

Mitigations: wired or own 5 GHz AP, code freeze a day before, two charged batteries (vendor says ~2 h), one person holding the remote, even overhead lighting, and pre-recorded voice lines for the long-latency path.
open_questions: Does Gemma 4 E2B audio work correctly on the G1's Orin NX with llama.cpp CUDA (JetPack 6.2, sm_87)? Jetson AI Lab flags an unspecified E2B audio issue. Test: build current llama.cpp with CUDA arch 87, run llama-mtmd-cli with the ggml-org BF16/Q8_0 audio mmproj on jfk.wav and a 5 s Mandarin/Spanish clip, compare text and RTF to faster-whisper base; also send input_audio to llama-server with max_tokens 200 and check for leaked thinking tokens / HTTP 500.

Memory budget on the 16 GB Orin NX: Gemma 4 E2B + audio+vision mmproj + KV cache + ASR fallback + TTS + robot services (Marvik and unitree_converse both hit OOM events). Test: run all services together for 30 minutes under tegrastats and log peak RAM.
Gemma 4 'pointing' output format is undocumented. Test: prompt 'point to the red can' on 20 table images and see whether it returns a point key or box_2d; decide whether box centers suffice.

Real Orin NX frame rates for NanoOWL (ViT-B/32 TensorRT engine) and YOLO-World worldv2 TensorRT: no published numbers. Test: build each engine, measure 100 frames at 640 px; drop them if Gemma 4 box_2d at 140-280 tokens is under ~0.6 s on the NX.

Is the G1 onboard mic stream usable after beamforming/AEC? Test: record 30 s from the multicast stream while standing, walking and speaking at 2 m; compute SNR and run ASR; if WER is poor, order the ReSpeaker XVF3800 and a UAC wireless lavalier and confirm each appears in `arecord -l` on the Jetson.

Which hands does our G1 have (Dex3-1, Dex5, none) and can they hold a soft can with a simple close command? Test: ExecuteAction and the Dex3 DDS example with the robot in debug mode, then a manual can placement into the hand.
Can the D435i be read from PC2 under JetPack 6.2 (pyrealsense2 depth + color aligned)? Test: realsense-viewer and a 10-line pyrealsense2 script; if USB3 fails, try a USB2 hub as the forum workaround.
Does LocoClient.WaveHand()/ShakeHand() actually move the arm on our firmware (community PR reports a no-op)? Test on day one; fall back to G1ArmActionClient ids 1/4.

Does the xr_teleoperate G1_29ArmIK accept a static end-effector target at 30 Hz without XR hardware, and how stable is a reach to a point 40 cm in front at table height? Test in the Unitree Isaac Lab sim first, then on the robot in damping-guarded mode.

Which languages will judges actually speak, and does the shipped quant handle them: measure Gemma 4 ASR on 5 clips each of zh/ja/es/hi/ko and listen to Piper vs Kokoro output for each before choosing TTS.

Whether a SeeDo-style learn-from-watching plan is reliable with Gemma 4 E2B/E4B instead of GPT-4o (SeeDo's open-source VLM baselines scored near zero). Test: record 5 short pick-place videos, extract 3-5 hand-speed keyframes, ask Gemma 4 for the step list, score against ground truth; if under ~60%, present it as 'narrate and point' rather than execute.

Whether the hackathon's 'runs on the device in front of you' rule accepts the MacBook tethered by Ethernet as the compute for the robot, which would remove most Orin latency and memory risk; ask the organizers before deciding the Orin-vs-Mac split.

checks.claim: Gemma 4 E2B/E4B accept audio natively (ASR + speech-to-translated-text) via a 305M USM-style Conformer encoder, 40 ms chunks of 16 kHz audio, 30 s max per clip; FLEURS WER 0.080/0.065 (en) and 0.090/0.075 (12-language avg); CoVoST BLEU 35.4/38.2.
checks.note: Official model card (ai.google.dev and HF google/gemma-4-E2B-it): audio on E2B, E4B and 12B Unified only; 'Audio supports a maximum length of 30 seconds'; ASR template 'Transcribe the following speech segment in {LANGUAGE} into {LANGUAGE} text.' and an AST template; encoder listed as 'about 300M'. Gemma 4 Technical Report (arXiv 2607.02770, v1 2 Jul 2026): 'E2B and E4B Gemma models use a 305M audio encoder that processes audio in 40ms chunks with Mel filterbank inputs', 'based on the Universal Speech Model' (2 downsampling convs + 12 Conformer layers); FLEURS table matches the claim exactly (E2B en 0.080, avg 0.090; E4B en 0.065, avg 0.075; ko/ja/zh reported as CER) and CoVoST X->en BLEU 35.4 / 38.2. The report states 16 kHz explicitly only for the 12B encoder-free path, but HF transformers' Gemma4AudioFeatureExtractor defaults sampling_rate=16000, max_length=480000 samples (= 30 s), audio_ms_per_token=40, audio_seq_length=750, which settles the rate. Caveat: the model card's headline FLEURS numbers (E2B 0.09, E4B 0.08) are 12-language averages, not English, and the card does not name the metric. The 12B Unified handles audio without a separate encoder (linear projection of waveforms).

verify.corrections: All six claims survive, but four planning assumptions must change. (1) Nobody has demonstrated Gemma 4 audio on an Orin NX: Marvik's conversational G1 ran Whisper, the LLM and TTS on an external 2x A40 host with only wake-word, mic and speaker on PC2; every llama.cpp audio report is x86 CUDA or Apple Metal; and NVIDIA's recipe flags an undated E2B audio problem under llama.cpp (cause unknown; its JetPack 6 images b8966/b9066 postdate the April fix). Validate on-Orin ASR first, with a USB mic (Marvik found the onboard array unusable), a BF16/F16 mmproj and thinking off. (2) Containers: `ghcr.io/nvidia-ai-iot/llama_cpp:latest-jetson-orin` now resolves to a JetPack-7 image (r38.2, CUDA 13), outside the JetPack 6 CUDA compatibility table; pin `b9066-r36.4.tegra-aarch64-cu129-22.04` (CUDA 12.9 toolkits are supported on the JetPack 6 driver). (3) TensorRT Edge-LLM needs JetPack 7.2; JetPack 7.2.1 does list the Orin family, so it is reachable, but only by reflashing Unitree's PC2 image six days out, which is not worth the risk. (4) The no-cloud rule: Unitree's `voice` service exposes TtsMaker and a `rt/audio_msg` ASR topic, but nothing documents where that ASR/TTS runs; prove it works with WAN unplugged or avoid it, using Gemma 4 ASR plus a local TTS (Piper, as unitree_converse does) through PlayStream (16 kHz mono int16). Smaller fixes: llama-server ignores `input_audio.format`; mics and speaker are standard on every G1, not EDU-only; no pointing output format exists anywhere, so plan on box_2d only; at the 70-token budget detection misses objects in clutter, so budget 140-280 tokens or crop for table scenes (the harness's 100% is one large fridge). Unverified: the NVIDIA forum NanoOWL latencies (HTTP 403), and web search was unavailable this run, so all checks used direct fetches.

research.digest:
What the partner awards actually are. The event page lists cash only for Best in Show (Android/Pixel), the two tracks and LiteRT; the partner prizes are hardware (5x Pi 5, 5x Coralboards, 2x Pixel 11, two Qualcomm packages) and none of them has published criteria. Nvidia and Synaptics are sponsors without their own award; Synaptics' award is in effect the Coralboard, since the new Coralboard is a Synaptics SL2619 board carrying Google Research's Coral NPU. The old Edge TPU line is legacy (edgetpu repo archived Apr 19, 2026), so an old Coral USB stick would not count as "Coralboard". Nothing says loaners will be available: bring everything.

What runs where, with numbers. Raspberry Pi 5 is Google's reference LiteRT IoT board. Gemma 4 E2B via LiteRT-LM on the Pi 5 CPU does 99-133 tok/s prefill and 7.6-9 tok/s decode in about 1.4-1.5 GB, with TTFT around 8 s for a 1024-token prompt, so prompts must stay short; Gemma 3 270M does 23-39 tok/s decode in 680 MB. The CLI takes .jpg/.wav attachments (`--attachment`, `--audio-backend=cpu`), has function calling (`--preset`), MTP, and an OpenAI-compatible `serve`. The GPU path exists but is slower than CPU for these models. The AI HAT+ 2 (Hailo-10H, $130) has no Gemma in its zoo, was measured slower than the Pi CPU for LLMs, and Google says LiteRT/Gemma on Hailo is only "coming soon"; buy it only if you want YOLO at 30 fps, and even then the AI Camera ($70) or the Pi CPU (YOLO26n at 101 ms) is simpler. The Coralboard ($99.79, 396 in stock at DigiKey, mic add-on $31) has two A55 cores, 1 TOPS NPU, 2 GB and Yocto; Gemma 3 270M is advertised out of the box, but no public document shows it on the NPU and the Torq compiler docs only show vision models, so expect CPU-speed 270M and a Yocto learning curve. The UNO Q ($79, in stock) runs Gemma 3 1B on four A53 cores at 5.5 tok/s through App Lab's llama.cpp brick with no NPU; it is a real-time I/O board (STM32 side) more than an AI board. The VENTUNO Q is the only Qualcomm part that runs Gemma 4 on an NPU (LiteRT-LM lists Dragonwing IQ8 at 3,747/31.7 tok/s and GenieX supports QCS8275), but it is a $299 pre-order with 3-4 week delivery, so it is unobtainable by Oct 24. Pixel 11 ($899, on sale since Aug 20) has a published Tensor G6 NPU bundle for Gemma 4 E2B and Tensor SDK v2.1 (Oct 14) support; it belongs to the Android/Pixel area but is the only hardware purchase with five-figure upside. Recommendation. Keep the humanoid demo as the single story and let partner hardware play a role the story needs, never a side demo. Two integrations are cheap and credible: (1) a Pi 5 16 GB as the robot's "concierge badge / charging-dock face": USB mic plus small screen, Gemma 4 E2B via LiteRT-LM doing wake-word-gated, short voice intents (multilingual, audio-in native) and passing structured requests to the G1 over local Wi-Fi, with the Pi showing the face/transcript. Cost about $330 (Pi 16 GB, case, mic, display), 6-10 hours, and it doubles as LiteRT evidence because LiteRT-LM is Google's showcase on this exact board. (2) Pixel 11 as the human-facing handset running the Tensor G6 bundle: that is the Android/Pixel area's call, but from a stacking view it is the only extra device whose award money exceeds its cost. Treat the Coralboard as optional: 8-15 hours, prize value about $500, plausible roles are a keyword-spotting or tiny-intent sensor node (Gemma 3 270M) on the fridge or door that pings the robot; only do it if a teammate owns it end to end and the board arrives by Tuesday. Treat the Qualcomm package as a lottery: criteria unknown, the VENTUNO Q cannot arrive, and a UNO Q running Gemma 3 1B at 5.5 tok/s would look like padding unless it has a natural job (the STM32 side driving an LED-matrix face or gripper sensors with Modulinos, the Linux side narrating with 270M); 6-10 hours, moderate distraction risk. Skip AI HAT+ (any version), Synaptics Astra Machina, Snapdragon laptops/phones and anything Nvidia-specific: no award, no Gemma advantage, or no time.

Cost/benefit, one line each. Raspberry Pi award: Pi 5 16 GB + mic + display, ~$330, 6-10 h, low distraction (it is the voice front-end the demo needs anyway), also feeds LiteRT. Coralboard award: $100-130, 8-15 h, medium distraction (Yocto/Torq), small prize. Qualcomm award: UNO Q $79, 6-10 h, medium-high distraction, unknown criteria; VENTUNO Q impossible in time. Pixel/TPU award: $899, 15-25 h, low distraction if the phone is the user's interface, but it competes with the robot for the narrative in Best in Show judging. Nvidia: $0, 0 h, nothing to win. Method note: the shared WebSearch budget was already exhausted when this check ran, so every verdict rests on direct fetches of the official pages, GitHub and the live event page (loaded in the browser pane because the AGI House site is a JS app). Five claims hold; one is partly wrong.

What the planning team must change:

1. Coralboard: Gemma 3 270M does run on the Coral/Torq NPU in Google's own demos (translation, scene transcription), and FunctionGemma 270M runs via llama.cpp on the A55 at ~9.7 tok/s with ~1.3–2 s per voice turn. A "Best Use of Coralboard" entry is therefore feasible from the public sl2610-examples repo, but the generic Torq compiler docs only test CNNs, no tok/s is published for the NPU path, and nothing mentions Gemma 4. Budget a day to reproduce the demo before committing. The board is $99.79 and in stock at DigiKey today, though Google's page still says "wait list".

2. Jetson/LiteRT: the GPU backend on Orin is not a dead end. Google's model card benchmarks Orin Nano GPU at 1,142 prefill / 24.2 decode, and a Sep 2026 Orin NX 16 GB report says --backend=gpu works once the prebuilt linux_arm64 libraries are on LD_LIBRARY_PATH (packaging bug, unverified by maintainers). 3. Prize facts: both tracks' first place get the "Break Glass" trophy; Qualcomm values ($1,350 / $450 per member) are stated on the page; first-place prizes ship later; bring your own robot, no loaners mentioned.

4. CLI hygiene: `litert-lm` (official PyPI, Python 3.10+) and `litert lm` (litert-cli/-nightly, used in the Pi posts) are different packages; backend flags auto-select since v0.14.0; tool calling over `litert-lm serve` is undocumented.

5. AI HAT+ 2 still has no Gemma path (zoo 5.1.1, no Hailo mention in LiteRT 2.3.0 / LiteRT-LM 0.18.0); use the Pi 5 CPU with LiteRT-LM (99/9 tok/s E2B, faster than llama.cpp's 58/7) for the Raspberry Pi award.
